issues.description: Log handler discovery by isinstance scan complects buffer-replay with global handler-list state
issues.detail: _flush_early_log_buffer walks logging.getLogger().handlers looking for a LoggingHandler instance, and _shutdown_telemetry does the same to remove it. The identity of 'the OTLP handler' is implicit — it's whatever LoggingHandler happens to be on root at the moment of the scan. If init_recording is called twice, if another library installs its own OTLP LoggingHandler, or if handler ordering changes, the wrong handler gets picked or removed. The value here (the OTLP sink we installed) and the identity (a reference we can later flush/remove) should be the same named thing. Capture the handler reference at install time in _setup_cloud_tracer and pass it back; don't rediscover it by type scan.

issues.description: _BufferingHandler buffer is an unbounded mutable place with no time semantics
issues.detail: self.buffer: list[logging.LogRecord] is a place-oriented, unbounded accumulator. If session.start() never happens and the process lingers (or recording is disabled mid-run via the init_recording early-return that calls _stop_log_buffering without replay), the buffer is silently dropped — fine. But if startup hangs while logs keep flowing, this grows without bound. LogRecord also retains references to args, exc_info tracebacks, and frame locals; held indefinitely this is a real memory and lifetime hazard. Either bound it (ring buffer with a documented cap) or make the time window explicit (last N seconds). The essential question — 'how much pre-start log history do we owe the server?' — should be answered in data, not left implicit.

issues.description: Three overlapping lifecycle methods on JobContext complect 'install', 'tear down', and 'flush+tear down'
issues.detail: _start_log_buffering, _stop_log_buffering, and _flush_early_log_buffer(replay=...) are three methods over one piece of state (self._early_log_handler) with overlapping responsibilities. _flush_early_log_buffer(replay=False) is operationally identical to _stop_log_buffering. The control flow in _on_cleanup -> init_recording -> _flush_early_log_buffer(replay=True), versus init_recording's early-return branch calling _stop_log_buffering, versus the cleanup-time fallback that synthesizes a RecordingOptions(logs=True) — these are several code paths reasoning about the same state transition. Collapse to one operation that takes the destination (None = drop, handler = replay-then-drop). The state machine is simple; the API around it is not.

issues.description: Cleanup-path synthesizes a RecordingOptions to trigger a side effect — complecting policy with mechanism
issues.detail: _on_cleanup calls init_recording(RecordingOptions(audio=False, traces=False, logs=True, transcript=False)) purely to drive the OTLP setup and flush. RecordingOptions is a user-facing policy value ('what did the operator ask us to record?'); using it as a control-flow lever for crash-log upload conflates two concerns. The PR description says 'we'll always upload crash logs but still honor user-specified record settings' — but the code path here ignores user settings on crash by hardcoding logs=True. Either that's intentional (then say so in a named function like _force_crash_log_upload()) or it's a bug. Don't smuggle the decision through a synthesized options struct.

issues.description: _shutdown_telemetry mutates the global root logger handler list as a side effect of shutdown
issues.detail: The new code in _shutdown_telemetry iterates root.handlers[:] and removes every LoggingHandler before force_flush. This is a global, place-oriented mutation justified by a deadlock comment. The deadlock is real (logs emitted during export re-enter the handler), but the fix complects 'shutdown the provider' with 'mutate everyone's root logger.' A handler that the application installed independently would also be removed. Prefer: install the OTLP handler under a filter that drops records during shutdown, or detach only the specific handler instance we installed (see issue #1 — same root cause: we never captured the identity of what we installed).

issues.description: Unrelated changes bundled: -n auto removed, test_plugin_google_stt removed, worker.py message ordering swap
issues.detail: The makefile drops parallel test execution and excludes a plugin test; worker.py reorders queue_msg vs pending_assignments registration. None of these are explained by 'upload crash logs.' Each may be correct on its own merits but they're complected into a feature PR, which makes the diff hard to reason about as a single value. The worker.py change in particular looks like a real race fix (register the future before announcing availability, so an immediate assignment can't miss the slot) and deserves its own commit and its own justification.

issues.description: _on_entry_done forces _shutdown_fut on crash but the elif-branch warning is now unreachable when an exception is also present
issues.detail: The previous log_exception had two independent branches: exception logging, OR the 'not connected and not shutdown' warning. The new _on_entry_done preserves that elif structure, which is correct, but the new behavior — force-setting _shutdown_fut on exception — means the await self._shutdown_fut below now resolves with a synthesized _ShutdownInfo whose reason is the string 'job crashed' regardless of the actual exception type or message. The value of 'why did this shut down' is being thrown away at the boundary. Carry the exception (or at least its repr) in the ShutdownInfo so downstream cleanup and telemetry can see what actually happened, instead of a constant string.

issues.description: process_closed emitted from a new code path without documenting whether listeners expect both init-failure and normal-close semantics
issues.detail: The proc_pool change emits process_closed when initialization fails, in addition to the existing close paths. The test in test_ipc.py was updated to handle proc.pid being None (because an uninitialized process has no pid yet). The event 'process_closed' is now overloaded across two regimes — 'ran and exited' vs 'failed to initialize' — which the listener has to disambiguate by checking pid. Either rename the new emission (process_init_failed) or document that process_closed listeners must handle the pid-is-None case. Right now the value of the event has been quietly broadened.

review.summary: The crash-log-upload feature is the right idea — pre-buffer logs early, replay them once the OTLP sink exists — but the implementation complects several concerns that should be separated. The identity of "the OTLP handler we installed" is never captured as a value; instead it's rediscovered by isinstance-scanning the global root logger in two places, which is fragile and makes the shutdown-time handler purge a blunt instrument. The buffering handler is a place-oriented unbounded list with no time semantics. Three methods (start/stop/flush) overlap over one piece of state and one of them — the cleanup-path synthesis of a RecordingOptions — uses a user-policy value as a control-flow lever, which is exactly the kind of "easy not simple" pattern that hides intent. The PR also bundles unrelated changes (makefile parallelism, a worker.py race fix, a test exclusion) that should have shipped separately. Decision: COMPLECTED — the underlying state machine ("buffer until sink exists, then drain or drop") is simple, but the code around it isn't yet.
